It names both specific persons (Thomas Flynn, Patrick Flynn), the specific alternative relationship (uncle, not father), and includes geographic detail (Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania) and temporal anchors (1850, 1860 census years). A follow-up search could directly test this claim against baptismal records, wills, or immigration documents.

dimensions.name: Evidence linkage
dimensions.rationale: All linked assertions are directly relevant to the hypothesis. Supporting assertions a_004 and a_010 (census co-enumeration in 1850 and 1860) are correctly linked as consistent with the uncle hypothesis—household position alone does not prove paternity. Contradicting assertion a_013 (death certificate naming Thomas as father) is correctly linked as direct contradiction to the uncle claim. The response explicitly explains why a_013 contradicts the uncle hypothesis despite the secondary informant caveat. No tangential or off-topic assertions are included.

dimensions.name: Status transitions
dimensions.rationale: The status transition is correct per research-schema-spec.md §5.9. The new hypothesis h_002 is set to active (not supported or ruled_out) because it has no direct positive evidence—only indirect evidence (census co-enumeration) that is equally consistent with both the father and uncle hypotheses. The contradicting assertion (a_013) prevents the hypothesis from being marked supported. The ruled_out flag is correctly false because there is no affirmative refutation, only a secondary-source contradiction. h_001 remains supported and unchanged, which is correct—creating a competing hypothesis does not downgrade the existing one.
